extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, including how to assess species/genus claims, examiner burdens, and appropriate office actions. Intended for use during patent examination, amendment review, priority/benefit determinations, and interference proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors showing possession of claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors. Factors to be considered include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement varies with nature and scope of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and what the level of knowledge and skill is in the art. In mature technologies where skill/knowledge are high, a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention. (See In re Hayes example: disclosing a capable microprocessor may suffice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater disclosure required in emerging or unpredictable arts
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not support a product claim (other than product-by-process). Where process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; but if it is not clear the acts can be performed or product produced, requirement may not be satisfied. Partial structure without additional characterization may not be sufficient (see Amgen). Reduction to practice can be the only evidence corroborating conception/possession in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claims must meet applicable tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references specific tests (i)(A), (i)(B), (i)(C) (e.g., reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or identifying characteristics). If a species claim fails those tests, reject for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims: representative number of species or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant, identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties), or by functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure, or by combination of such characteristics sufficient to show possession of the claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' means the species adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation. If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected. (Cites: Eli Lilly, Enzo, Noelle, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: One species may sometimes support a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only one species within a genus adequately describes a claim to that genus only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are situations where one species adequately supports a genus (examples: Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe) — e.g., when the skilled person would understand that variation among species is unimportant for the claimed invention's operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-number standard depends on predictability and skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes a 'representative number' is an inverse function of the skill and knowledge in the art. Satisfactory disclosure depends on whether one of skill would recognize that the applicant was in possession of the necessary common attributes/features of the genus members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For unpredictable arts, adequate written description of a genus embracing widely variant species cannot be achieved by disclosing only one species. In predictable arts, less may be required (e.g., amino acid sequence discloses nucleic acids encoding it because genetic code is known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot support overly expansive claim language by describing only one embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language and satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 'merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand that the applicant had invented, and was in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed. (Cites: LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy and examiner's initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed to be adequate unless or until sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary is presented. The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in an applicant's disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy. See In re Marzocchi and Wertheim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required findings when rejecting for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact to support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supportable by the application, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for new or amended claims / entitlement to earlier priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present in the original written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. If the original disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected or the priority denied. (Cites: Hyatt v. Boone, In re Wright, In re Robins, In re Smith, In re Robertson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant reply / reexamination before repeating rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, examiners must re-determine patentability in view of the whole record, including amendments, arguments, and any evidence submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If not, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal, and properly treat further showings (analyze affidavits relevant to 112, para. 1). (See In re Alton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and clear communication in office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and review proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing any rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions, and reasons which support them, and when possible offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession (acceptable forms of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Cites: Pfaff, Regents of Univ. of California v. Eli Lilly, Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter need not be described literally; inherency and implicit description
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of a claim need not be described literally (i.e., using the exact words) for the disclosure to satisfy the description requirement; implicit or inherent support may sometimes be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. If a claim is amended to include subject matter not present in the application as filed, examiner should conclude the claim is not described and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph or deny benefit of filing date as appropriate. (Cites: In re Robertson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Common procedural circumstances raising written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues most typically arise in certain circumstances: amendments affecting a claim, reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120, reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119, and support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these contexts, ensure that claims are supported in the earlier or original disclosure in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. (Cites: Wright, Tronzo, Scheiber, Ziegler, Kawai, Gosteli, Hyatt.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case factual inquiry; examiner burden reiterated
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the description requirement is met must be determined on a case-by-case basis and is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must present a reasonable basis and preponderance of evidence to rebut the presumption of adequacy. (Cites: In re Wertheim.)
